newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia mulls programs to fight social ills.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia mulls programs to fight social ills.

text.p: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Wednesday urged the country's Moslem leadership to find ways to fight social problems affecting Moslems, saying the government would consider a national social service programme.

"This idea was mentioned by one of the speakers from the floor that we should have some kind of national service... and that is something the government will consider," Mahathir told reporters after meeting about 1,000 religious leaders, some Moslem Cabinet ministers and state chief ministers.
He gave no details on the shape the programme.
Mahathir said on Friday the country's Moslem leadership was planning "to launch a campaign to fight against the spread of social ills".
Over the past few months, multicultural Malaysia has been engaged in a fresh morality drive among its 21 million people, the majority of whom are Moslem.
It is cracking down on video arcades, ordering nightclubs and karaoke lounges to close earlier and warning about the dangers of "punk" culture among its youth.
The crusade has coincided with an operation against illegal immigrants, who have been blamed for a host of ills, including crime and the spreading of infectious diseases.
The vast majority of the immigrants are from Indonesia, which has lately witnessed an upsurge in Moslem unrest.

The Moslem leadership is concerned about the involvement of Malays, who are all Moslem, in social problems such as incest and drug-taking. Most of the 200,000 heroin addicts are Malays, the Home Ministry has said.

"We acknowledge in almost all the social problems in the country, Malays form the majority. This is very embarrassing," said Abdul Hamid Othman, minister in the Prime Minister's Department, in an interview published in the Star newspaper on Wednesday.
Abdul Hamid said a recent study on incest showed Moslems were involved in 90 percent of the reported cases.
Although often an acerbic critic of the West and its ways, Mahathir told the forum that foreign influences could not be shut out of the country, adding: "We do not blame others".
Mahathir did not mention the unrest among Indonesian Moslems in his hour-long speech to the conference. It was not clear if it was discussed in closed-door discussions afterward.
Improving the content of Islamic education might be one way to curb social problems in Malaysia, Mahathir said.
"Maybe it's the failure of the content," he said. "What did we actually teach when we teach them about religions? Was it enough just to teach others how to pray and perform religious obligations?"
Abdul Hamid told reporters that the campaign against the social ills would be aimed at Moslem youth, but that the amount of funding for the programme was not yet decided.
